source.title: At the Edge of Understanding: Sparse Autoencoders Trace The Limits of Transformer Generalization
source.authors: Praneet Suresh; Jack Stanley; Sonia Joseph; Luca Scimeca; D. Bzdok

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present and usable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE-based representation measurements to transformer models, including Llama 3.1 8B, and reports feature-activation results relevant to indirect LLM evidence; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own SAE-feature activation measurements relevant to V4. Results from cited work are not recorded. MMLU accuracy, jailbreak mitigation, fine-tuning outcomes, and OOD energy-score comparisons are omitted because they do not directly measure the claim versions. Closed-source model performance is not evidence about internal feature representation.
record.test_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders as a tool to detect out-of-distribution inputs. It assumes that SAEs 'learn a useful approximation' of the model's representation space. It never tests whether that holds. Its results are counts of active SAE latents, reconstruction-error energy scores, fine-tuning losses and jailbreak rates on OOD versus in-distribution inputs. None of these bears on whether features are superposed, whether neurons are polysemantic, whether an SAE recovers the model's true sparse features, or whether features are 1-D. More SAE latents firing on typo or jailbreak inputs says nothing about whether superposition holds; the study's own method performance is what is being reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that OOD inputs (typos, style shifts, successful jailbreaks) make transformers activate more, largely spurious SAE concepts and raise reconstruction error. An SAE-derived energy score detects this shift and selects better fine-tuning samples. Aligning SAE activations via LoRA cuts jailbreak success from 46% to 7% with only a 0.09% MMLU drop, and improves Spoken-SQuAD exact match. They stress that their method relies on global SAE properties, not canonical individual features.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders to measure feature activations and OOD shifts in trained transformers; it does not use the original toy-network superposition setup or test feature-vector geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-activation measurements vary with input condition, including typo rate and jailbreak outcome. The paper reports that SAE-derived results are broadly similar across random SAE initializations and that OOD classifications agree across GPT-2 layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Across three random SAE initializations on GPT-2 layer 6, aggregate energy-score distributions and fine-tuning results were 'nearly identical'. The authors say this holds despite individual features differing, but they do not measure feature overlap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregate SAE statistics (L0, reconstruction error) are stable across SAE seeds even when individual features are not canonical.

fits_no_version.finding: OOD inputs (typos, style shift, successful jailbreaks) raise the SAE L0 and reconstruction error in GPT-2 (25M) and Llama 3.1 8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The number of active SAE latents and the reconstruction error increase on out-of-distribution inputs.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 306, 2026)
record.problems: The paper assumes the SAE is a useful approximation of transformer representations. Individual feature canonicality is not independently tested; the authors note that the learned feature sets can differ across initializations. Internal processes of the OpenAI models were inaccessible. Some feature-count evidence is presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant feature-count results left out. Other reported OOD, benchmark-performance, fine-tuning, and jailbreak-defense results do not measure the representation claims in these versions.

untested.parts: No toy models of sparse features versus dimensions; no tests of geometry or phase transitions.
No analysis of neurons, polysemanticity or capacity competition.
Does not test whether features are spread across neurons, and does not validate that the SAE latents are the model's features. SAEs are used as an assumed approximation.

Cites the non-canonicality of individual SAE features (Leask et al.; Paulo & Belrose). Its own retraining check (three SAE initializations, App. A.6.1) compares only energy-score distributions and fine-tuning curves, not feature identity, completeness or stability.

record.verdict_notes: Elhage et al. 2022 is cited only as background for the linear representation hypothesis. The reader's V4 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels should be dropped: feature-count increases on OOD inputs do not test whether superposition holds. R4's comparison uses latents selected by correlation with jailbreak success, so it is partly circular.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test superposition geometry, feature sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy networks.
Does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or polysemantic neurons.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.

Measures SAE-encoded feature activations, not feature distribution across neurons or whether the SAE features are ground-truth model features; internals of GPT-4o mini and GPT-5-thinking-nano were inaccessible.
Does not directly test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; it discusses non-canonicality and reports stability of aggregate SAE-derived results across initializations.
Does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Counted unique active SAE features over input sequences as typo rates increased.

conditions.value: 0% to 100% of words; one typo per selected word
50 TinyStories validation samples; 50 random typo configurations

rows.measure: Average number of unique active SAE features
rows.baseline: Clean input; numeric feature count not stated
rows.value: At 100% typo words, nearly 30% more features on average than clean input
rows.uncertainty: Figure 1 reports a shaded 1 standard deviation; deviations described as very small across typo configurations.
rows.note: The text describes feature count as growing almost monotonically and near linearly as typos increase.
rows.check: Counts unique active SAE latents in GPT-2 layer 6 as the typo rate rises. This measures the OOD signal of the authors' detector, not V4. V4 asks whether LLMs contain sparse features an SAE can recover; the SAE is assumed, and its recovery of true features is not validated. Values are correct: nearly 30% more features at 100% typos, Section 4.1, Fig 1B.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE-identified concept activations in MMLU question prompts as typo rates increased.
rows.measure: Number of active SAE concepts in prompts
rows.baseline: Normal, typo-free prompts (figure baseline; numeric value not stated)
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2B shows averages across 5 random typo configurations; uncertainty magnitude not stated in text.
rows.note: The text says OOD perturbations activate a large number of potentially distracting concepts compared with the normal baseline.
rows.check: Same problem as R1 for Llama 3.1 8B layer 19 on MMLU (Goodfire SAE). The result is figure-only and is a detector property, not evidence on superposition or SAE recovery.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Counted activated SAE features in MMLU-CF prompts as typo rates increased.
rows.value: Up to 10.2% activated at 75% typo rate
rows.note: The paper describes the increase as replicating the OOD-induced feature-activation pattern.
rows.check: The measure is the percent increase in 'prompt insensitive' SAE features versus the 0% baseline, up to about 10% at a 75% typo rate. The caption is Figure 19(b); the text calls it Figure 20B. This is a detector property, not a test of any version.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Counted final-token activations among the 100 SAE concepts most correlated with jailbreak success.
rows.measure: Average number of the top 100 success-correlated SAE concepts activated
rows.note: The authors also state that raw L0 values were consistently higher for successful jailbreaks, but give no separate numeric value for that comparison.
rows.check: Compares successful and unsuccessful jailbreaks on the top-100 success-correlated latents: 10.2 vs 5.3. These latents are selected by correlation with the outcome, so the gap is partly built in by selection. It is not a measure of superposition or of SAE feature recovery.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT-2 typo-corrupted inputs and Llama 3.1 8B MMLU, MMLU-CF, and jailbreak prompts
reader_labels.reason: SAE measurements identify active sparse features in transformer activations, with feature counts increasing for typo-corrupted inputs and successful jailbreak prompts (R1–R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SAE-based measurements in the tested models
reader_labels.reason: The measurements establish properties of SAE codes, but do not independently validate that those codes are the model’s true features or show how features are distributed across neurons (R1–R4).
